newsitem.title: USA: Tasty but ugly sea creatures coming to U.S. stores.
newsitem.headline: Tasty but ugly sea creatures coming to U.S. stores.

text.p: Dave Johns concedes the Goeduck clam "looks obscene" but says "it's really tasty" and can win over Americans' palates if given time. The oversized clam with a neck like an elephant's trunk is already a delicacy in Japan, where it can sell for up to $15 a pound ($33 per kg) and is usually served raw, he said. "Most of our harvest, I'd say 90 to 95 percent of it, is exported to Japan," said Johns, whose company Taylor Shellfish Farms of Shelton, Washington, is one of 750 exhibitors at the International Boston Seafood Show that runs through Thursday. The Goeduck, pronounced "gooeyduck," grows only in the waters off Alaska, Canada and Washington State. Divers harvest the clams, which can grow as large as 15 pounds (6.8 kg), using pressure water jets. "I personally don't eat it raw," Johns said. "Now if you ask me how I eat it, I'll tell you -- in stews and chowder." The Seafood Show, bringing together distributors, shippers, exporters and packagers from 25 countries hawking everything from herring to halibut, has expanded the definition of seafood to include items usually found growing in deserts. "Aloe vera is the newest product and, frankly, I think it's hot," Azuma Foods International, Inc. marketing director Devan Nielsen said as he handed out samples of the vegetable, which grows in sandy soil and has a light, fruity taste. The plant, a traditional remedy for burns, is processed at the company's plants in Oakland, California and Nagoya, Japan. "This can be used in salads or served with sorbet," Nielsen said, adding that it would be marketed directly to consumers at the retail level. "Well, it will be more expensive than canned peaches, but it's a completely different product. A little more upscale." Azuma, a Japanese company that opened its U.S. branch in 1989, also offers whelk and baby octopus along with seaweed and flying fish roe to U.S. consumers. Whelk, a snail harvested in North American waters, "is a hot concept food," Nielsen said. "It's really big in Europe and here in the U.S. you'll find it being served at white linen restaurants from Maine to Miami and even Omaha." Seafood, he said, is a global business. "The fisherman at the dockside in rubber boots knows exactly what the price of tuna is in Japan at any given moment." Fishermen in Canada's Prince Edward Island, where Steve Fortune and his brothers own Atlantic Aqua Farms, have a tougher job harvesting sea scallops, oysters and mussels. Wearing thick wetsuits, divers plunge through holes cut in the three-foot (one metre) thick ice to harvest the shellfish. "You couldn't get the quality of these mussels in the wild. They're sand-free, grit-free and we ship them 365 days a year," Fortune said.
